headings.title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Oesophagus
headings.content: The oesophagus is a muscular tubular organ approximately 25 centimetres long in adults, extending from the pharynx down to the stomach. Functionally, its primary role is to transport ingested food and fluids from the oral cavity and pharynx into the stomach via coordinated peristaltic contractions. The wall of the oesophagus consists of four main layers: the mucosa, submucosa, muscularis layer (composed of an inner circular and outer longitudinal muscle layer), and adventitia. The upper third of the oesophagus contains striated skeletal muscle, while the lower two-thirds transition into smooth muscle. At the junction between the pharynx and the oesophagus lies the upper oesophageal sphincter (UOS), which prevents air from entering the gastrointestinal tract during respiration. At the distal end, the lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) acts as a high-pressure zone that serves as a physiological valve, preventing the retrograde flow of acidic gastric contents back into the sensitive squamous epithelial lining of the oesophagus. Coordination of these structures is regulated by the autonomic nervous system, specifically the vagus nerve, ensuring efficient swallowing without aspiration. Understanding this basic anatomy and physiology is crucial for nursing students, as alterations in muscular tone, sphincter competence, or mucosal integrity form the foundation of all major oesophageal pathologies encountered in clinical practice across Nigerian healthcare settings.

headings.title: Assessment and Diagnostic Procedures for Oesophageal Disorders
headings.content: Assessment of patients presenting with oesophageal disorders requires a thorough clinical history focusing on symptoms such as dysphagia (difficulty swallowing), odynophagia (painful swallowing), pyrosis (heartburn), regurgitation, and water brash. Nurses must evaluate the onset, duration, and aggravating or relieving factors of these symptoms. Diagnostic procedures are critical for confirming underlying aetiologies. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, also known as oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD), remains the gold standard diagnostic tool. It allows direct visualisation of the mucosal lining, detection of inflammation, ulcers, strictures, or varices, and facilitates tissue biopsy for histopathological examination. Barium swallow radiography provides real-time fluoroscopic imaging of the swallow mechanism, highlighting structural abnormalities, strictures, hiatus hernias, or motility disorders like achalasia. Oesophageal manometry measures the intraluminal pressure and coordinated muscular contractions of the oesophagus and its sphincters, which is essential for diagnosing motility disorders. Additionally, 24-hour ambulatory pH monitoring measures the frequency and duration of acid exposure in the lower oesophagus, aiding in the definitive diagnosis of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. Nursing responsibilities during these diagnostics include patient preparation, obtaining informed consent, monitoring vital signs post-procedure, and ensuring airway safety, particularly after sedated endoscopic procedures.

headings.title: Gastro-Oesophageal Reflux Disease (GORD) and Hiatus Hernia
headings.content: Gastro-Oesophageal Reflux Disease (GORD) occurs when gastric contents chronically flow backward into the oesophagus, causing troublesome symptoms and potential mucosal damage. The primary mechanism is transient or permanent incompetence of the lower oesophageal sphincter. Contributing factors include delayed gastric emptying, increased intra-abdominal pressure (from obesity or pregnancy), and dietary habits. A common anatomical partner to GORD is a hiatus hernia, where a portion of the stomach herniates upward through the diaphragmatic hiatus into the thorax. Hiatus hernias are classified mainly as sliding (Type I, where the gastro-oesophageal junction displaces upward) or paraoesophageal (Type II, where part of the stomach pushes up alongside the oesophagus). Clinical manifestations of GORD include pyrosis, chest pain that can mimic cardiac events, regurgitation, chronic cough, and hoarseness. Complications if left untreated include bleeding, oesophageal strictures, and Barrett’s oesophagus—a premalignant condition where normal squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar epithelium. Management involves lifestyle modifications such as weight loss, elevating the head of the bed, avoiding late-night meals, and dietary adjustments. Pharmacological therapy utilizes antacids, H2-receptor antagonists (e.g., famotidine), and proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) like omeprazole to reduce gastric acidity. Severe cases may require surgical interventions such as laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication to restore lower oesophageal sphincter competence.

headings.title: Oesophagitis and Oesophageal Ulceration
headings.content: Oesophagitis refers to inflammation of the mucosal lining of the oesophagus, most commonly resulting from chronic acid reflux, but it can also be caused by infections (such as Candida albicans in immunosuppressed patients), caustic ingestions, or medications (like NSAIDs or potassium supplements) that become lodged in the lumen. When mucosal injury progresses deep into the submucosa and muscular layers due to persistent chemical or infectious insult, oesophageal ulceration occurs. Patients with oesophagitis and ulcers frequently present with severe odynophagia, retrosternal chest pain, dysphagia, and occasional haematemesis or melaena if bleeding develops from the base of the ulcer. Nursing assessment focuses on evaluating pain characteristics, nutritional intake, and signs of gastrointestinal bleeding. Management depends on the underlying cause. For reflux-induced oesophagitis, aggressive acid suppression with proton pump inhibitors is standard. Infectious oesophagitis requires targeted antimicrobial or antifungal therapy (e.g., oral fluconazole for candidiasis). Patients who ingest caustic substances must never be induced to vomit; instead, they require emergency evaluation, serial endoscopic assessments to grade tissue injury, and prevention of long-term stricture formation through careful medical and surgical follow-up. Nurses play a vital role in patient education regarding medication adherence, dietary modifications to avoid spicy and acidic foods, and monitoring for warning signs such as sudden severe pain or signs of perforation.

headings.title: Oesophageal Motility Disorders: Achalasia and Spasms
headings.content: Oesophageal motility disorders are characterised by abnormal peristalsis and impaired relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter. The classic motility disorder is achalasia, a condition marked by the degeneration of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus of the oesophageal wall, leading to failure of the lower oesophageal sphincter to relax during swallowing and complete absence of normal peristalsis in the smooth muscle oesophagus. This creates functional obstruction, causing progressive dysphagia for both solids and liquids, nocturnal regurgitation of undigested food, weight loss, and retrosternal chest pain. Barium swallow often demonstrates a characteristic 'bird-beak' tapering at the distal oesophagus with proximal dilation. Other motility disorders include diffuse oesophageal spasm (DES), characterised by uncoordinated, simultaneous, high-amplitude contractions causing severe chest pain and dysphagia. Management of motility disorders aims to reduce lower oesophageal sphincter pressure to allow gravity-assisted emptying of the oesophagus. Therapeutic options include oral calcium channel blockers or nitrates, endoscopic injection of botulinum toxin into the LOS, pneumatic balloon dilation, or surgical myotomy (Heller myotomy) where the muscle fibres of the lower sphincter are cut. Nursing care involves monitoring nutritional status, managing symptoms post-procedure, providing small, frequent soft meals, and educating patients on eating slowly and drinking plenty of water with meals.

headings.title: Oesophageal Varices and Management of Bleeding
headings.content: Oesophageal varices are dilated, tortuous submucosal veins in the lower oesophagus resulting from portal hypertension, most commonly caused by advanced liver cirrhosis. When portal pressure rises, blood is diverted from the portal system into lower pressure collateral venous circulations, including the coronary veins of the stomach and the lower oesophageal veins. These fragile vessels have thin walls and are prone to rupture, leading to massive, life-threatening upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage presenting as haematemesis (often bright red), melaena, and signs of hypovolaemic shock. Management of bleeding oesophageal varices is a medical and nursing emergency requiring simultaneous resuscitation and intervention. Nurses must immediately secure large-bore intravenous access, administer crystalloids and blood products as prescribed, monitor vital signs continuously, and maintain airway patency, especially if the patient has altered consciousness from hepatic encephalopathy. Medical management includes vasoactive drug infusions (such as octreotide or somatostatin) to reduce splanchnic blood flow and portal pressure, along with prophylactic antibiotics to prevent spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Urgent endoscopic therapy is performed to achieve haemostasis via endoscopic variceal ligation (EVL) or sclerotherapy. In refractory cases, balloon tamponade (using a Sengstaken-Blakemore tube) or transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) procedures may be utilised to decompress the portal system. Strict monitoring of intake and output, neurological checks, and psychological support for the patient and family are vital nursing responsibilities.

headings.title: Oesophageal Tumours and Carcinoma
headings.content: Oesophageal tumours can be benign, but malignant tumours—specifically oesophageal carcinoma—represent significant health challenges associated with high morbidity and mortality. The two main histological types of primary malignant oesophageal tumours are squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma. Squamous cell carcinoma typically arises in the upper and middle thirds of the oesophagus and is strongly associated with risk factors such as smoking, heavy alcohol consumption, ingestion of hot liquids, and nutritional deficiencies. Adenocarcinoma predominantly occurs in the lower third of the oesophagus and is closely linked to chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and Barrett's oesophagus. The hallmark symptom of oesophageal carcinoma is progressive dysphagia, starting with difficulty swallowing solids and gradually advancing to semi-solids and liquids. Other clinical features include significant unexplained weight loss, odynophagia, hoarseness (due to recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement), persistent cough, and iron deficiency anaemia from chronic occult bleeding. Diagnosis is confirmed via upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsy and brush cytology. Staging requires computed tomography (CT) scans of the chest and abdomen, endoscopic ultrasound (EUS), and positron emission tomography (PET) scans. Treatment options depend on the stage and may involve a combination of surgical resection (oesophagectomy), chemotherapy, and radiotherapy. Nursing care involves comprehensive nutritional support (often via feeding tubes or parenteral nutrition), rigorous pain management, psychological support, and palliative care for advanced, non-resectable cases.

headings.title: Nursing Care and Patient Management in Oesophageal Disorders
headings.content: Nursing care and patient management for individuals with disorders of the oesophagus requires a holistic, patient-centred approach encompassing assessment, symptom management, nutritional support, psychological care, and patient education. Because many oesophageal conditions impair swallowing and nutritional intake, nurses must closely monitor body weight, dietary tolerance, and serum albumin levels. Enteral nutrition via nasogastric or feeding gastrostomy/jejunostomy tubes may be necessary, and nurses are responsible for administering feeds safely, monitoring for aspiration, and maintaining tube patency. For patients undergoing surgical interventions such as oesophagectomy or fundoplication, postoperative nursing care is critical. This includes close monitoring of respiratory status and chest tube drainage, pain management using patient-controlled analgesia (PCA), early mobilization, and careful advancement of the diet once anastomotic integrity is confirmed. Patient education focuses on lifestyle modifications, such as eating smaller, frequent meals, avoiding recumbency for at least two to three hours after eating, elevating the head of the bed, quitting smoking, and reducing alcohol intake. Nurses also educate patients on medication compliance, recognising red-flag symptoms such as severe chest pain, worsening dysphagia, or signs of bleeding, and ensuring regular follow-up appointments to monitor disease progression or recurrence.
